lesson.title: Project clinic: turn a topic into a falsifiable research question
lesson.timeMeaning: Suggested independent study minutes; not scheduled contact time
lesson.lead: “Use a GPU for databases” is a topic. A research question names a mechanism, a comparison, a workload and a possible failure.
goals: Write a bounded research claim with a falsification condition.
Connect a proposed mechanism to an observed bottleneck.
Prepare concrete evidence and decisions for an instructor consultation.

sections.title: Start here: prerequisites and course status
sections.html:
“I want to study vector databases” names a topic, but does not tell us what result could change our mind. We will turn it into a question using one mechanism: waiting briefly to search several incoming queries together.

Bring one mechanism from lessons 28–31. The charter below is an original planning example, not a measured research result. This supplemental clinic is not an Edinburgh lecture or verified Canvas assignment. Instructor appointments, required deliverables, assessment rules and deadlines remain unverified.

sections.title: The research-question contract
sections.html:
Imagine queries arrive one at a time and the GPU spends much of its time waiting. A small waiting window might collect several queries and use the device better. But the first query must now wait for the others. We have a possible benefit and an immediate cost, so we can ask: under what arrival rates does batching improve throughput while staying within a p95 response-latency budget?

Here p95 is the response time at the declared 95th percentile; state how it is computed. Fix the dataset, hardware, metric and recall target. Compare immediate dispatch and a tuned batching baseline. Write what would count against the proposal: no benefit at matched p95, or recall below target.

This makes the claim falsifiable: an allowed observation can show it false. An implementation milestone such as “build an ANN server” cannot do that. The output of the project can be a bounded operating range, including losing cases, rather than a universal win.

Key takeaway

A narrow question with a credible baseline is stronger than a broad system with no testable claim.

sections.title: Use a causal chain to justify the mechanism
sections.html:
Before building, trace the suspected cause: tiny batches → little parallel work per launch → low device utilization → a waiting window may increase batch size → queue delay may increase response time. Each arrow needs evidence, not just a plausible story.

Record batch sizes, utilization, queue delay, device execution and arrival-to-response latency. If preprocessing on the host is already the bottleneck, faster device search may barely change the user's wait. A minimal prototype should test the most uncertain arrow first; a short feasibility time box is a planning choice, not a course deadline.

Turn “LLMs improve query optimization” into a testable question.

For example: on held-out multi-table templates, can an LLM choose among the same ten legal plans faster end to end than the native optimizer, including selection time and without extra timeouts? Add a simple non-LLM ranker. This fixes decision, domain, candidates, baseline, cost boundary and failure condition.

sections.title: Build a literature-and-evidence matrix
sections.html:
A related paper is useful when it can change a project decision. For each close paper, record exact title, venue/year and publication status, then problem, assumption, mechanism, strongest baseline, workload, metric, artifact and limitation. Finish with “what differs from my question?” and “what would reproducing this require?”

For our batching question, a paper may report high throughput only for large preformed batches. That supports the device mechanism but does not measure how long online users wait to form a batch. A learned-optimizer paper's random query split may likewise not answer unseen-template generalization.

Keep author-reported measurements separate from your own. An arXiv manuscript can be an accepted paper when a primary record confirms acceptance; otherwise label its actual status. This bibliography is supplemental and does not invent an instructor-assigned reading list. Reading the protocol as carefully as the abstract prevents borrowing a claim under incompatible conditions.

Sources for this section: Is Your Learned Query Optimizer Behaving As You Expect? A Machine Learning Perspective; NVIDIA cuVS: Benchmarking methodologies. Numerical traces marked original are teaching examples, not reported measurements.

sections.title: Worked example: a one-page research charter
sections.html:
Write the charter in the order a reader needs. Question: when does microbatching improve end-to-end ANN throughput under a p95 budget? Motivation: preliminary traces suggest low batch-1 utilization, which must be measured. Mechanism: cap how long a query waits while arrivals accumulate. Baselines: immediate dispatch and tuned fixed-size batching with identical search parameters.

Vary arrival rate, waiting cap and difficulty; hold dataset, GPU and quality target fixed. Collect queue and execution time, arrival-to-response p50/p95/p99, QPS, recall and failures. Falsification: gains disappear at matched p95 or difficult queries miss the recall target. Deliver a reproducible plot showing both useful and losing regimes.

Finally inspect the load generator. A closed-loop client sends the next request only after a reply; slowing the server reduces offered load and can hide queue growth. An open-loop client schedules arrivals independently. Choose the model matching your claim, verify the generator keeps up, and record dropped or failed arrivals. Otherwise a queueing result may really describe the client.

sections.title: Prepare an instructor consultation that can change the project
sections.html:
A consultation should resolve a decision, so bring the one-sentence question, bottleneck trace, closest paper and precise difference. Add one preliminary result or failure with configuration and uncertainty. Ask two concrete questions, such as whether the baseline is fair and whether scope should prioritize filtered recall or freshness.

After the discussion, record the actual advice, evidence, decision, owner and next check. An informal suggestion does not become a grading rule. Follow actual appointment and document instructions when provided.

The proposal needs four GPUs but only one is available. What is a rigorous rescope?

Study a single-device mechanism or an explicitly controlled model of communication overhead and narrow the claim accordingly. Do not call it reproduction of four-device scaling. Record the resource limit and ask whether the narrowed question fits the instructor's real expectations. A smaller answer supported by evidence is more useful than an untestable large promise.

Key takeaway

Bring a decision and the evidence needed to make it, rather than a list of activities.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest project starting point?
options: Build the fastest possible database.
Use every available GPU.
Implement a paper without reading its evaluation.
Test a specific mechanism against a fair baseline under a stated workload and constraint.
quiz.explanation: A testable claim connects scope, mechanism and evidence; implementation size alone does not make a research contribution.

questions.question: Which element makes a research hypothesis falsifiable?
options: A condition under which evidence would contradict it.
A promise to use the newest model.
A sufficiently ambitious title.
A large number of implementation files.
questions.explanation: A falsifiable hypothesis specifies an observable failure condition, not just the desired result.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: What should an instructor consultation ideally bring?
options: Invented grading criteria.
Only a broad topic name.
Concrete evidence, a scoped question and decisions that need guidance.
An untested claim of success.
questions.explanation: A consultation is more useful when the instructor can evaluate a choice using actual assumptions and evidence. Required formats remain instructor-specific.

questions.question: A project needs four GPUs but one is available. Which response preserves scientific integrity?
options: Pretend the one GPU is four devices.
Hide the hardware configuration.
State that four-GPU scaling is proven analytically without a model.
Narrow the question to a single-device mechanism and disclose the new scope.
questions.explanation: Rescoping is legitimate when the revised evidence matches the revised claim. Do not claim measurements from unavailable hardware.

questions.question: How should an arXiv paper with no verified venue acceptance be labeled?
options: As assigned course reading.
As a preprint until acceptance/publication is verified from a reliable primary record.
As peer-reviewed whenever code is public.
As a SIGMOD paper if its topic is databases.
questions.explanation: Repository availability and subject area do not establish acceptance or assignment status.
